DIRECTOR AND OFFICER INDEMNIFICATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Corp.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE — DIRECTOR AND OFFICER INDEMNIFICATION INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet relates to Acme Corp., a California corporation, and describes California Corporations Code section 317 in full: the statute governing when Acme Corp. may, or must, indemnify a director, officer, employee, or other agent for costs and liability arising out of that role, the statute's own procedure for deciding whether indemnification is proper in a specific case, and the statute's separate authorization for Acme Corp. to purchase director and officer liability insurance.

This project's existing Corporate Bylaws document already includes three clauses drawn from this same statute — the general permissive indemnification power, the mandatory rule for an agent successful on the merits, and the expense-advancement mechanism. This information sheet is meant to accompany, not replace, that treatment: it restates those same statutory subdivisions for a reader who wants this single topic addressed on its own, and it adds three subdivisions the Corporate Bylaws document's clauses do not reach — the statute's own definitions, the full standard specific to a derivative action (a suit by or in the right of the corporation), the statutory approval procedure naming who may authorize indemnification in a specific case, the statute's limits on when indemnification is barred outright, and the corporation's separate power to purchase and maintain director and officer liability insurance.

This information sheet is educational only. It states what the statute provides; it does not determine whether Jane Doe is, or was, entitled to indemnification or insurance coverage for any specific proceeding, and it is not a substitute for Acme Corp.'s own bylaws, articles, or any separate indemnification agreement, which may set different or additional terms within what the statute allows.

WHO AND WHAT THE STATUTE COVERS — STATUTORY DEFINITIONS
Section 317 defines three terms that control how far it reaches. "Agent" is defined broadly: it covers a person who is or was a director, officer, employee, or other agent of the corporation, and it extends to a person serving at the corporation's request as a director, officer, employee, or agent of another corporation, partnership, joint venture, trust, or other enterprise, and to a person who held one of those roles with a predecessor corporation or enterprise at that predecessor's request. "Proceeding" is defined to include a threatened, pending, or completed action or proceeding of any kind — civil, criminal, administrative, or investigative — not just a completed lawsuit. "Expenses" is defined to include, without limitation, attorneys' fees, plus the expenses of establishing a right to indemnification under the statute's mandatory-indemnification rule or under a court application for indemnification. This information sheet uses these three terms as the statute defines them wherever they appear below, in connection with Jane Doe's role at Acme Corp.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "For the purposes of this section, “agent” means any person who is or was a director, officer, employee or other agent of the corporation, or is or was serving at the request of the corporation as a director, officer, employee or agent of another foreign or domestic corporation, partnership, joint venture, trust or other enterprise, or was a director, officer, employee or agent of a foreign or domestic corporation which was a predecessor corporation of the corporation or of another enterprise at the request of the predecessor corporation; “proceeding” means any threatened, pending or completed action or proceeding, whether civil, criminal, administrative or investigative; and “expenses” includes without limitation attorneys’ fees and any expenses of establishing a right to indemnification under subdivision (d) or paragraph (4) of subdivision (e)."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 317(a) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, statutory definitions of "agent," "proceeding," and "expenses" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=317.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory subdivision, Corporations Code section 317, subdivision (a); it is not an independent source and should not be read as corroborating the other clauses in this information sheet, which quote other subdivisions of this same section. This clause states the statute's definitions themselves; it does not determine whether a particular director, officer, employee, or other agent in fact falls within the statutory definition of "agent" for any specific proceeding, nor does it address how a court has applied these definitions to a disputed set of facts — no case law is cited or verified anywhere in this document. The definition of "expenses" cross-references two other subdivisions of this same section (the mandatory-indemnification rule and the court-application approval method) rather than standing alone; both are addressed in this information sheet's other clauses.

INDEMNIFICATION
Acme Corp. may indemnify a director, officer, employee, or other agent who is or was a party to a legal proceeding because of that role, against expenses, judgments, fines, and settlements actually and reasonably incurred, if that person acted in good faith and in a manner reasonably believed to be in the corporation's best interests — and, in a criminal proceeding, had no reasonable cause to believe the conduct was unlawful.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "A corporation shall have power to indemnify any person who was or is a party or is threatened to be made a party to any proceeding (other than an action by or in the right of the corporation to procure a judgment in its favor) by reason of the fact that the person is or was an agent of the corporation, against expenses, judgments, fines, settlements, and other amounts actually and reasonably incurred in connection with the proceeding if that person acted in good faith and in a manner the person reasonably believed to be in the best interests of the corporation and, in the case of a criminal proceeding, had no reasonable cause to believe the conduct of the person was unlawful."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 317(b) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, permissive power to indemnify (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=317.)
  "No indemnification shall be made under this subdivision for any of the following: (1) In respect of any claim, issue or matter as to which the person shall have been adjudged to be liable to the corporation in the performance of that person’s duty to the corporation and its shareholders, unless and only to the extent that the court in which the proceeding is or was pending shall determine upon application that, in view of all the circumstances of the case, the person is fairly and reasonably entitled to indemnity for expenses and then only to the extent that the court shall determine."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 317(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, derivative-suit limitation on indemnification (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=317.)
  Known gap: This power is permissive under this statute — it authorizes indemnification but doesn't by itself require it; a corporation that wants indemnification to be guaranteed, not discretionary, typically has to say so explicitly in its own bylaws or a separate agreement. A real, important limitation: this specific rule is narrower for a proceeding brought by or in the right of the corporation itself (a derivative suit) — indemnification for amounts a person is found liable to the corporation for is barred in that kind of case unless a court specifically determines the person is fairly and reasonably entitled to it, even where the general good-faith standard above would otherwise be met. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what indemnification powers and limits typically look like — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 317) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

WHEN INDEMNIFICATION ISN'T OPTIONAL
Everything above is a power Acme Corp. may exercise, not a promise — except in one specific situation, where indemnification stops being discretionary: if a director, officer, employee, or other agent is successful on the merits in defending a proceeding (or a specific claim or issue within it), the corporation must indemnify that person for the expenses actually and reasonably incurred defending it.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "To the extent that an agent of a corporation has been successful on the merits in defense of any proceeding referred to in subdivision (b) or (c) or in defense of any claim, issue, or matter therein, the agent shall be indemnified against expenses actually and reasonably incurred by the agent in connection therewith."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 317(d) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, mandatory indemnification for success on the merits (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=317.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine mandatory floor underneath the general discretionary indemnification power — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. "Successful on the merits" is a narrower outcome than simply avoiding liability (for example, a case settled or dismissed on procedural grounds may not qualify), so this mandatory right shouldn't be assumed to cover every favorable outcome. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 317(d)); no additional independent source was found for this.

A DIFFERENT STANDARD FOR A DERIVATIVE ACTION — A SUIT BY OR IN THE RIGHT OF THE CORPORATION
Section 317 sets two different permissive standards depending on who the proceeding is against whom. For a third-party proceeding — one not brought by or in the right of the corporation itself — this project's existing Corporate Bylaws document already describes the statute's good-faith standard, under which Acme Corp. may indemnify Jane Doe against expenses, judgments, fines, and settlements. A derivative action is different: where the proceeding is brought by or in the right of Acme Corp. itself to procure a judgment in Acme Corp.'s favor, the statute allows Acme Corp. to indemnify Jane Doe only for expenses actually and reasonably incurred defending or settling that action — not for judgments, fines, or settlement amounts owed to the corporation — and only if Jane Doe acted in good faith, in a manner Jane Doe believed to be in the best interests of Acme Corp. and its shareholders. Unlike the third-party standard, this derivative-action standard has no separate "no reasonable cause to believe the conduct was unlawful" prong tied to a criminal proceeding, because a derivative action is a civil suit by the corporation's own shareholders on the corporation's behalf, not a criminal prosecution.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A corporation shall have power to indemnify any person who was or is a party or is threatened to be made a party to any threatened, pending, or completed action by or in the right of the corporation to procure a judgment in its favor by reason of the fact that the person is or was an agent of the corporation, against expenses actually and reasonably incurred by that person in connection with the defense or settlement of the action if the person acted in good faith, in a manner the person believed to be in the best interests of the corporation and its shareholders."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 317(c) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, permissive indemnification standard for a derivative action (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=317.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the introductory standard of Corporations Code section 317, subdivision (c) — a different subdivision from the ones already quoted in this project's Corporate Bylaws document, which quotes subdivision (b) in full and only the first limitation, paragraph (1), of subdivision (c), not this introductory standard sentence. Both are subdivisions of the same statutory section rather than independent sources. This clause states the derivative-action standard itself; it does not restate the separate, further limitations on derivative-action indemnification found later in subdivision (c) — including the bar on indemnifying a person adjudged liable to the corporation absent a specific court determination, already quoted in this project's Corporate Bylaws document, and two additional bars (on amounts paid settling a pending action without court approval, and on expenses of defending a pending action settled without court approval) that no clause in this corpus currently quotes. This clause does not determine whether any specific proceeding against a given director or officer is, or was, a derivative action within the meaning of this subdivision.

WHO DECIDES — THE STATUTORY APPROVAL PROCEDURE FOR A SPECIFIC CASE
Outside the mandatory rule for an agent successful on the merits, section 317 does not let indemnification happen automatically just because the good-faith standard could be met — the statute requires that indemnification be authorized in the specific case, upon a determination that Jane Doe met the applicable standard, and it names four specific ways that determination can be made: (1) a majority vote of a quorum of Acme Corp.'s directors who are not themselves parties to the proceeding; (2) if such a quorum cannot be obtained, a written opinion from independent legal counsel; (3) approval by Acme Corp.'s shareholders, with any shares owned by Jane Doe not entitled to vote on the question; or (4) the court in which the proceeding is or was pending, on application by Acme Corp., Jane Doe, or the attorney or other person who rendered the defense services, whether or not Acme Corp. opposes that application.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Except as provided in subdivision (d), any indemnification under this section shall be made by the corporation only if authorized in the specific case, upon a determination that indemnification of the agent is proper in the circumstances because the agent has met the applicable standard of conduct set forth in subdivision (b) or (c), by any of the following: (1) A majority vote of a quorum consisting of directors who are not parties to such proceeding. (2) If such a quorum of directors is not obtainable, by independent legal counsel in a written opinion. (3) Approval of the shareholders (Section 153), with the shares owned by the person to be indemnified not being entitled to vote thereon. (4) The court in which the proceeding is or was pending upon application made by the corporation or the agent or the attorney or other person rendering services in connection with the defense, whether or not the application by the agent, attorney or other person is opposed by the corporation."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 317(e) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, statutory approval procedure for indemnification in a specific case (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=317.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory subdivision, Corporations Code section 317, subdivision (e); it cross-references, but is not itself, the good-faith standards of subdivisions (b) and (c) described elsewhere in this information sheet and in this project's Corporate Bylaws document. No clause currently in this corpus quotes this approval-procedure subdivision, so this is new coverage rather than a restatement. This clause states the four statutory approval methods themselves; it does not determine which method, if any, a given corporation has in fact used or would use for a specific proceeding involving a specific director or officer, and it does not address how a corporation's own bylaws might elaborate on this procedure (for example, by specifying which officer calls a vote) beyond what the statute itself requires.

ADVANCING DEFENSE COSTS
Acme Corp. may pay a director, officer, employee, or other agent's litigation expenses as they're incurred, before the proceeding is even over, rather than waiting to reimburse them only after a final determination that indemnification is proper. That advance comes with a condition: the person receiving it must first agree, in writing, to repay the money if it turns out later that they weren't actually entitled to be indemnified.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "Expenses incurred in defending any proceeding may be advanced by the corporation prior to the final disposition of the proceeding upon receipt of an undertaking by or on behalf of the agent to repay that amount if it shall be determined ultimately that the agent is not entitled to be indemnified as authorized in this section."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 317(f) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, advancement of defense expenses (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=317.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a genuine mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific corporation. Like the general indemnification power itself, advancement here is something the corporation may do, not something it automatically must do, unless the corporation's own bylaws or a separate agreement commits to it. This is a single statutory subsection (§ 317(f)); no additional independent source was found for this.

WHEN INDEMNIFICATION IS BARRED OUTRIGHT
Section 317's permissive indemnification power and its approval procedure both give way to two specific bars. Except for the mandatory-indemnification rule and a court's own application-based approval, Acme Corp. may not indemnify or advance expenses to Jane Doe where doing so would be inconsistent with a provision of Acme Corp.'s own articles, bylaws, a shareholder resolution, or an agreement that was in effect at the time the underlying claim accrued and that prohibits or otherwise limits indemnification, or where it would be inconsistent with a condition a court expressly imposed in approving a settlement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "No indemnification or advance shall be made under this section, except as provided in subdivision (d) or paragraph (4) of subdivision (e), in any circumstance where it appears: (1) That it would be inconsistent with a provision of the articles, bylaws, a resolution of the shareholders, or an agreement in effect at the time of the accrual of the alleged cause of action asserted in the proceeding in which the expenses were incurred or other amounts were paid, which prohibits or otherwise limits indemnification. (2) That it would be inconsistent with any condition expressly imposed by a court in approving a settlement."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 317(h) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, statutory bars on indemnification or advancement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=317.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory subdivision, Corporations Code section 317, subdivision (h); no clause currently in this corpus quotes it. This clause states the two statutory bars themselves; it does not determine whether a given corporation's own articles, bylaws, or any agreement in fact contain a provision that limits or prohibits indemnification, and it does not address subdivision (g) of this same section, which separately allows a corporation's articles to authorize indemnification rights broader than this statute's own default permissive power — a distinct, additional mechanism this clause does not describe.

SEPARATE STATUTORY AUTHORIZATION TO PURCHASE DIRECTOR AND OFFICER LIABILITY INSURANCE
Apart from indemnification itself, section 317 separately authorizes Acme Corp. to purchase and maintain liability insurance on behalf of Jane Doe against liability asserted against, or incurred by, Jane Doe in that role or arising out of that status — and this insurance-purchasing power exists whether or not Acme Corp. would actually have the power to indemnify Jane Doe against that same liability under the rest of this statute. In other words, D&O insurance can reach some liability that the indemnification provisions above would not permit Acme Corp. to cover directly out of its own funds.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A corporation shall have power to purchase and maintain insurance on behalf of any agent of the corporation against any liability asserted against or incurred by the agent in that capacity or arising out of the agent’s status as such whether or not the corporation would have the power to indemnify the agent against that liability under this section."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 317(i) (California Legislative Information text), California General Corporation Law, authorization to purchase director and officer liability insurance (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=317.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the core authorizing sentence of Corporations Code section 317, subdivision (i); it is a single statutory subdivision, not an independent source corroborating the other clauses in this information sheet. This clause does not quote or address the remainder of subdivision (i), which imposes conditions on a corporation's power to purchase insurance from a company the corporation itself wholly or partly owns (an affiliated or "captive" insurer) — conditions this clause does not describe and that a corporation considering that kind of arrangement would need to review separately. This clause also does not address subdivision (j), which excludes certain employee-benefit-plan fiduciary proceedings from this section and instead cross-references a different statute, Corporations Code section 207, subdivision (f) — that cross-referenced statute was not independently fetched or verified for this document. Nothing here states whether a given corporation has purchased, or is required to purchase, any insurance policy.

CLOSING AND SIGNATURE BLOCK — DIRECTOR AND OFFICER INDEMNIFICATION INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet regarding Acme Corp. was prepared by John Smith.

Executed on January 1, 2026 at Los Angeles, California.

Signature: _________________________

[This information sheet describes California Corporations Code section 317 — mandatory and permissive director and officer indemnification, the different standards for a third-party proceeding and a derivative action, the statutory approval procedure, the statutory bars on indemnification, expense advancement, and the separate authorization to purchase director and officer liability insurance. It is not a completed indemnification agreement, a board or shareholder resolution, an insurance application, or legal advice, and it does not itself obligate Acme Corp. to indemnify, advance expenses to, or insure Jane Doe or any other agent. The current statutory text is published by the California Legislative Information website (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov).]

expectedJSON.body: Acme Corp. may pay a director, officer, employee, or other agent's litigation expenses as they're incurred, before the proceeding is even over, rather than waiting to reimburse them only after a final determination that indemnification is proper. That advance comes with a condition: the person receiving it must first agree, in writing, to repay the money if it turns out later that they weren't actually entitled to be indemnified.

expectedJSON.body: Section 317's permissive indemnification power and its approval procedure both give way to two specific bars. Except for the mandatory-indemnification rule and a court's own application-based approval, Acme Corp. may not indemnify or advance expenses to Jane Doe where doing so would be inconsistent with a provision of Acme Corp.'s own articles, bylaws, a shareholder resolution, or an agreement that was in effect at the time the underlying claim accrued and that prohibits or otherwise limits indemnification, or where it would be inconsistent with a condition a court expressly imposed in approving a settlement.

citations.case: Cal. Corp. Code § 317(h) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California General Corporation Law, statutory bars on indemnification or advancement
citations.quote: No indemnification or advance shall be made under this section, except as provided in subdivision (d) or paragraph (4) of subdivision (e), in any circumstance where it appears: (1) That it would be inconsistent with a provision of the articles, bylaws, a resolution of the shareholders, or an agreement in effect at the time of the accrual of the alleged cause of action asserted in the proceeding in which the expenses were incurred or other amounts were paid, which prohibits or otherwise limits indemnification. (2) That it would be inconsistent with any condition expressly imposed by a court in approving a settlement.

expectedJSON.body: Apart from indemnification itself, section 317 separately authorizes Acme Corp. to purchase and maintain liability insurance on behalf of Jane Doe against liability asserted against, or incurred by, Jane Doe in that role or arising out of that status — and this insurance-purchasing power exists whether or not Acme Corp. would actually have the power to indemnify Jane Doe against that same liability under the rest of this statute. In other words, D&O insurance can reach some liability that the indemnification provisions above would not permit Acme Corp. to cover directly out of its own funds.
